title: How to Find Mental Health Care, No Matter Where You Live
summary: Access to mental health care varies widely by state. Here's a practical, step-by-step guide to finding care, regardless of insurance, budget, or location.
body_markdown:
## How to Find Mental Health Care: A Step-by-Step Guide


Knowing why access varies doesn’t make care easier to find. These steps can help you get started:


1.


#### Start with your insurance plan, doctor, or employer.


If you have insurance, use your plan’s provider directory to find covered care. You can also ask your primary care doctor for help. Your doctor can also rule out any physical health issue that could cause your symptoms and refer you to a mental health provider. If you have a job, ask whether your employer offers an Employee Assistance Program (EAP). An EAP may provide a limited number of free, private counseling visits.


2.


#### No insurance doesn't mean you don’t have options.


Federally funded community health centers serve people even if they cannot pay the full cost. The amount you pay may be based on your income. Most offer virtual care, and[mental health needs make up 40% (4 in 10) of all telehealth visits](https://www.nachc.org/policy-advocacy/policy-priorities/telehealth/) at these centers.


SAMHSA's[FindTreatment.gov](https://findtreatment.gov/) is a free, private way to search licensed low-cost and sliding-scale facilities by zip code.


3.


#### Care matching tools can help you find the right care for you.


Rather than scrolling through dozens of provider bios trying to guess who's the right fit, many practices now offer[care matching tools](https://lifestance.com/book-appointment/) . These tools will ask about your needs, age, insurance, and whether you want online or in-person care. The tool will then show you providers who may meet your needs you can book with, making a long list easier to review.


4.


#### Learn about different types of providers.


Provider titles can be confusing. A psychiatrist is a medical doctor that can prescribe medication. A psychologist, LCSW, or licensed counselor provides therapy, and many individuals end up seeing more than one as part of their coordinated care plan.[LifeStance's guide to therapist types and credentials](https://lifestance.com/blog/therapist-types-credentials-explained-guide/#therapist-credentials-specializations-and-what-they-treat-reference-table) breaks down what each abbreviation means to help give you context before you start your search.


5.


#### Treat the first appointment as a conversation, not a commitment.


A first session often lasts 45–60 minutes. The provider will ask questions to learn about you and your needs. It is a conversation to see if they are the right fit, not a test. You may not feel comfortable with the first provider you meet. In fact,[4 in 10 adults](https://mhanational.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/State-of-Mental-Health-2025.pdf) report being unable to[find a provider](https://lifestance.com/provider/) that felt like the right fit. Know that you can switch providers or try a matching tool again with updated preferences. It’s common, not starting over from scratch.


The first provider you contact may not be the right fit. That's normal. The important thing is to keep moving forward until you find care that meets your needs.


**from a study of more than 139,000 patients analyzed by US Census region*
